title: Nonacute angles and defect matching
subtitle: G2 lecture 050000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Two closed subspaces can contain directions that meet at exactly ninety degrees.
body: The cosine on such a direction is zero. Consequently, the canonical projection-based intertwiner can have a kernel, and its polar factor is only a partial isometry: it cannot by itself transport those missing directions. To obtain a unitary direct rotation, the right-angle directions lost on one side must be matched with those lost on the other. That failure poses two questions. Can we supply the missing motion using the right-angle pieces? And if we can, is there still one preferred answer?

slides.title: The two crossed defects
slides.lead: Let U and V be closed subspaces, with projections P and Q.
body: Their four elementary intersection parts separate the cases where both projections agree from the crossed right-angle defects. The common part lies in both U and V. The exterior part lies perpendicular to both. Neither causes a problem for transport: on those spaces the direct rotation can act as the identity. The source defect consists of vectors in U that are perpendicular to V. The target defect consists of vectors in V that are perpendicular to U. These are the crossed right-angle directions. Call them D source and D target. They are orthogonal to one another.

slides.title: A right-angle plane
slides.lead: Take the horizontal line U and vertical line V in the ordinary plane.
body: Here P projects onto the horizontal direction, Q onto the vertical direction, and K is zero. You can check it immediately: projecting a horizontal vector into V gives zero, and projecting a vertical vector into V perpendicular also gives zero. So the polar factor of K is the zero operator. But the geometry obviously admits rotations from U to V. Rotate counterclockwise by ninety degrees, or clockwise by ninety degrees. Both work. The choice is a choice of how to match the horizontal source-defect line with the vertical target-defect line. A unit horizontal vector may be sent to either unit vertical vector.

slides.title: Build a quarter-turn from a matching
slides.lead: Now suppose the two defect spaces have the same Hilbert-space dimension.
body: That means we can choose a linear isometric equivalence J from D source onto D target. Use J to define the missing motion. On a source-defect vector x, send x to J x. On a target-defect vector y, send y to the negative of J inverse applied to y. What does this do to lengths? J preserves lengths, and J inverse does too. The two output spaces are orthogonal, so the map preserves the sum of squared lengths. It is unitary on the direct sum of the two defects. Apply the map twice. Starting in D source, the first step applies J and the second applies negative J inverse. The result is negative x.

slides.title: Complete the regular polar factor
slides.lead: Let R be the orthogonal complement of the sum of the two crossed defects.
body: Call it the regular part. On R, the polar factor of K preserves lengths. To understand why, recall that the polar factor is a partial isometry: it is an isometry on the orthogonal complement of K's kernel. The kernel is precisely the crossed-defect sum, so R is the initial space of the polar factor. For this particular K, the final space of the polar factor is also R. One way to see it is to study K adjoint, which interchanges the source and target projections but has the same crossed-defect kernel. The closures of the ranges of K and K adjoint are therefore both R.

slides.title: Why matching is necessary
slides.lead: Could some clever unitary avoid the matching requirement by mixing a defect direction with the regular part?
body: No, not if it satisfies the direct-rotation conditions. Those conditions constrain the positive diagonal blocks and the relation between the crossed blocks. The operator then has a Hermitian part determined by the positive cosine. On a crossed defect, that Hermitian part vanishes. Let x lie in the source defect. Because the direct rotation intertwines the projections, T x lies in V. Positivity of the diagonal compression, together with its zero quadratic form on this defect, forces the source component of T x to vanish. Hence T x lies in U perpendicular as well.

slides.title: An infinite-dimensional obstruction
slides.lead: It is worth seeing why counting the ordinary dimensions of U and V is not enough.
body: Take a Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis indexed by all integers, positive and negative. Let U be the closed span of the basis vectors with indices zero, one, two, and so on. Let V be the closed span of those with indices one, two, three, and so on. Both U and V are infinite-dimensional, and their orthogonal complements are infinite-dimensional too. A bilateral shift is a unitary map carrying U onto V. But the source defect is the line spanned by the basis vector with index zero. The target defect is zero, because V is contained in U. Those two spaces cannot be isometrically equivalent.

slides.title: What if the defects are finite?
slides.lead: For finite-dimensional defect spaces, isometric equivalence reduces to equality of dimensions.
body: Pick orthonormal bases of both defects. If their basis lengths agree, mapping one basis to the other defines J. If their dimensions disagree, no isometry onto can exist. A useful application occurs when the difference between P and Q is compact. The crossed defects are then eigenspaces of the compact self-adjoint difference, with eigenvalues plus one and minus one. Nonzero eigenspaces of a compact operator are finite-dimensional. So both defect dimensions are finite, even if U and V are infinite-dimensional. In that setting, numerical dimension equality really is enough to build the matching.

slides.title: Reconstruction
slides.lead: First, show that K kills both crossed defects, and explain why its kernel contains nothing else.
body: Second, write down a two-by-two ninety-degree rotation and identify the source-to-target map J and the negative reverse map. Third, prove that this quarter-turn is unitary on the defect sum, while the polar factor is unitary on its orthogonal complement. Combine them. Fourth, examine the integer-indexed basis example. Why does an ambient unitary exist while a direct rotation fails? The conclusion is precise. A nonacute direct rotation exists exactly when the two crossed right-angle spaces admit an isometric matching. The choice of matching controls the nonuniqueness.
